Canon 2562A002 EF 28-135mm f/3.5-5.6 is USM Standard Zoom Lens for Canon SLR Cameras The Canon 28-135mm f/3.5-5.6 lens with Image Stabilization is a very capable, and more importantly, affordable lens,and is perfect for times when you just want to have one lens on the camera but you also want to have a lot of options with your focal range. While you get the benefits of a slight wide to telephoto range in one handy package, you do lose in light stops as you move through the focal range (the maximum aperture stops down as you move toward the telephoto end of the range). This is where the image stabilization comes in very handy, and allows you to keep hand shake at bay even when you have to compromise on shutter speed to get the correct exposure.

I've had no complaints about the optical quality, I think you'll be pleased with the shots you get from it - the lens may be cheap but don't confuse that with what the quality of image this lens can provide. Keep in mind on a camera with a cropped sensor (any Canon DSLR model other than the 5D and 1D models) the focal range is equivalent to @45-215mm - you lose a bit of the wide angle advantage, but you get more telephoto, so it depends which end of the focal range you value the most as to whether that is a disadvantage or not.
text_fidelity_b: Canon 2562A002 EF 28-135mm f/3.5-5.6 is USM Standard Zoom Lens for Canon SLR Cameras

SUDOKEJI 1000W Pure Sine Wave Inverter Power Inverter Peak Power 2000W 12V DC to 110V 120V AC with LED Display 3 AC Outlets & USB Port for RV Truck Boat This worked just fine for powering a few small items. When choosing what you are going to run on this add up the total wattage of all devices, then add at least 50% more to account for peaks or spikes in the power draw. For example if your coffee maker draws 500 watts, your laptop 300 watts, and your toaster 200 watts (total, 1000 watts) you should account for the extra 50% (1000watts + 500 watts (the 50%)=1500watts). In this example, a minimum 1500 watt inverter should be used.

If the item is motor driven, it requires additional start-up (surge) wattage (typically 2-3 times the continuous wattage required) to start the device. For example, a miter saw that runs at 700 watts might require 1400 watts to start up. If your inverter only supplies 1000 watts, you will not be able to start it up. In this case, you would want to select an inverter rated at least 1400 surge watts to handle start-up needs.

I understand how wattage works and for someone who doesn't, any inverter could fail if overloaded with more power than it can handle. An overload feature that automatically shuts the device off would be helpful for anyone who is unsure. This has an overload feature, but if you blow a fuse, you'll have to replace it. Do your research and know how this works, and it'll work fine.
text_fidelity_b: SUDOKEJI 1000W Pure Sine Wave Inverter Power Inverter Peak Power 2000W 12V DC to 110V 120V AC with LED Display 3 AC Outlets & USB Port for RV Truck Boat

text_fidelity_a:
Click 'n Dig Model E4 Key Finder. 4 Receivers. Wireless RF Remote Item, Wallet Locator Okay, this is an update to the one-star review I emitted originally. The Click 'n' Dig folks are definitely getting their money's worth from their PR people, whom I would hire myself if I could afford to hire someone who works that hard. After viewing my crabby review (below), they got in touch and offered to send a new set (you get the key finder and several other pieces that you can attach to other easily lost items). Surely, said they, the set shipped to me must have been defective. Would I take another one and if it improved, would I consider re-reviewing?

Oh, why not? I have nothing else to do during the hours left around the seven 14-hour days a week entailed in running a business. :-D They sent the doodads in the mail.

MEANWHILE... Between the time I first posted my original grutch and the time the new package of goodies arrived, I lost my keys not once, not twice, but THREE TIMES.

Each time, the Key Finder located the things! Inside a purse...on a piece of furniture where I'd dropped the keys to rescue the dog...atop a countertop where no one in their right mind would ever leave their keys...

It's not a matter of standing wherever you happen to be and clicking the "finder" device. You do have to walk around the house, and you do have to point the finder in several directions until it locates and connects with the receiver on your keyring. Its signal will pass through some but not all walls (why, I do not know: possibly electrical wiring or insulation?). Its range is about 20 feet, I'd guess. It requires some patience and persistence on your part, but it does eventually work.

Click 'n' Dig sent me a new set, which I gave to some dear friends who are even more superannuated than I after the Missus expressed dismay at having lost her keys once again. This is one of those tools that makes old age tolerable...maybe even survivable.

***********

ORIGINAL WHINGE: Not sending this back, because I don't have time to hassle with repackaging and mailing. But can't recommend it. These devices are supposed to emit a 90-decibel beep when you point the hand-held radio transmitter at them. Thus if you have one on, say, a key ring, you should be able to locate the keys if you misplace them around the house. We're told the radio frequency goes through walls and has an 80-foot range.

Well, if that's 90 decibels, then 90 decibels isn't very loud. According to Purdue University, 90 db is as loud as a "Boeing 737 or DC-9 aircraft at one nautical mile (6080 ft) before landing (97 dB); power mower (96 dB); motorcycle at 25 ft (90 dB). Newspaper press (97 dB)." Dang! I wish!! If aircraft made the same level of sound as this handy-dandy beeper, the skies would be a lot quieter around here!! :-D And my neighbor's Harley would be a lot more fun, too...

No, the signal does not go through walls.

The range is about 25 feet. Any further away than that, and the transmitter will not elicit a beep. If your keys have dropped out of your pocket and slipped under a chair cushion, you have to be right on top of the chair to get receiver to beep.

Could be the gadgets need new batteries, which are kindly included. But the instructions do not show how to find the battery cases or how to open them. On the key fob, it's obvious enough where the battery case is, but you can't get it open -- I split a fingernail and hurt my finger when I tried. On the flat gadgets that you can stick to objects with the provided double-sided tape, I can't even find a CLUE to where a battery case could be opened. ?????????

The idea behind this device is truly brilliant. Sure do wish the execution were better.
text_fidelity_b: Click 'n Dig Model E4 Key Finder. 4 Receivers. Wireless RF Remote Item, Wallet Locator

text_fidelity_a:
Nitecore SC2 Superb Charger 3A Quick Charge Bundle with EASTSHINE EB182 Battery Organizer Overall, this is a solid charger. The build quality is top-notch, it’s sized so that you don’t have to struggle to put in/take out 26650s, and the 3A charge rate is a treat. However, it has a design issue that, while not a major roadblock, can be quite irritating.

Let’s start with the good news. This is one solidly-built charger. Compared with other chargers in its general price class from Efest and Xtar, this has a lot more heft to it. The sliders are perfect – not too loose; not too tight – and move smoothly without any crunchiness or squeaking. Best of all, it can hold two 26650s without any difficulty getting them in or out of the slots. That’s a great feature since I’ve been using a lot more 26650 mods recently, and getting those fat batteries in or out of some of my Xtar chargers is a major pain.

Other ease of use features include non-slip feet on the base that keep it firmly planted. The included power cord does not have a wall wart on the end – just a regular plug – which is a welcome change. All in all I have absolutely zero complaints about the fit and finish.

Performance is also solid. Each slot is independent, and can be set to charge at up to 3A. However, only one channel can be set at 3A since the total cannot exceed 5A. But even one 3A channel is a great feature if you use large capacity 26650s that can support a 3A input. It cuts the recharge time to the bone. It also has a USB output for charging (2.1A). However, you must leave slot 2 empty if you want the USB charging to take priority. Otherwise, it will charge the cell in slot 2 first, then charge via USB.

The charger has all the customary protection features that you would expect from a good quality charger such as overtime protection, reverse polarity protection, and auto shut off if it runs more than 10 hours. It also has a recovery mode for deeply discharged Li-ion cells. I never use that (if I accidently deeply discharge a cell I no longer use it) but it has the feature should it be of value for your needs. Heat output when running was very low.

The current for each slot can be set to 0.5A, 1A, 2A or 3A. You can also set the cutoff voltage to 1.2v, 3.7v, 4.2v or 4.3v. I use this nearly only with Li-ion cells, so the 4.2v cutoff is what I use for most of my charging. However, it’s nice to have the 3.7v setting for when I want to charge cells for long-term storage.

If you do nothing, the charger will set itself to a 2A current for cells that are greater than 1200mAh, and 0.5A for cells less than 1200mAh. You can override the settings for both current and cutoff independently for each channel.

And that’s where the biggest irritation occurs. The charger has a double row of LED lights that signify current and cutoff levels (plus blink to show operation, and stop blinking when charging is done). Simple and unobtrusive. However, there are no notations on the screen to show what charge rate/cutoff corresponds to each LED. Instead, those numbers are listed on a piece of clear plastic that is stuck on top of the display. It peels off easily and looks like a temporary cover to protect the screen.

In addition to looking poor, the lack of durability of the cover with the numbers listed means it won’t survive for long. Now, there are only four positions for the LEDs so it’s not a huge puzzler to decipher the settings if you use the charger regularly. However, I have several chargers and can go a couple of weeks between using one in particular. It can be hard to remember which LED position means what. And I shouldn’t have to do that – numbers should be imprinted right on the screen and not on a flimsy piece of plastic.

I also don’t care for the fact that the button labels (one for current, one for cutoff) are embossed into the plastic. The black-on-black makes it very hard to see which button is which.

But those issues aside, this is a solid charger that offers up to 3A charging. The build quality and operation are both excellent, and it’s perfectly sized to hold two 26650 cells without a bit of struggle to get them in or out of the slots. The poorly designed screen and button labels drops my score to 4.5 stars, but I’ll round up since everything else is well executed.
[Sample provided for review]
text_fidelity_b: Nitecore SC2 Superb Charger 3A Quick Charge Bundle with EASTSHINE EB182 Battery Organizer

text_fidelity_a:
Sony SRS-XB21 Portable Wireless Bluetooth Speaker, Black (SRSXB21/B) A very impressive looking speaker. The unit has good heft to it and if feels sturdy and it is exceptionally well constructed. It also sounds really good. At full volume it can easily fill a decent sized room with sound, the bass is clear, with great mid range and wonderful highs.

That being said, the speaker does have a lot of things wrong with it. First, the USB cable that comes with it is very short. It also doesn’t come with a power adapter, so you have to have an extra one around, which shouldn’t be a problem, but at this price, this speaker should come with a power adapter.

There are white lights on the front that bounce and light up and pulse to the music. Very cool for a party, but grows old quick. I was hoping to take this camping, but I don’t want dancing lights when I’m out in the woods. I can’t seem to find a way to turn them off. The instructions are very sparse and not helpful at all.

Even plugged in there is a unit time out where it powers down after so many minutes. I was hoping this would be a good external speaker for my Amazon Echo Dot, but that won’t work.

It also is supposed to have a feature where you tap (more like hit hard) the speaker for sounds like a high hat, cymbal, and Tom Tom. when it works, it’s pretty cool, but it seemed to only work intermittently. And in order for it to sound any good at all, you have to hit it very hard.

Connecting to it is easy. You can connect through your phone’s Bluetooth or tap your phone on it, if it has NFC, for even easier connections. It also has a aux port for connecting with an aux wire. Battery lasts a long time.

Overall it’s a good sounding speaker, and it’s well made. But be warned, depending on what you want it for, this may not be for you. The lights that won’t shut off and the unit time off (even when on external power) as well as the short power cable make me not recommend it to many people.
text_fidelity_b: Sony SRS-XB21 Portable Wireless Bluetooth Speaker, Black (SRSXB21/B)

CD player stopped working after 3 months (just spit out cds) and the sound stopped 2 weeks later. Thus one star. Prior to that I was happy with it, so here's my review.
***UPDATE***: While it was past the Amazon return date, it was within the OEM 1yr warranty, so I sent it back and they replaced it. I had to pay shipping to them and round trip was 2 to 3 weeks without a radio. In general I do like the unit for the money, so long as this one isn't a dud.

Installation wasn't bad. I didn't need a trim kit as the one it came with was fine. I purchased a wire harness for my Nissan Frontier and crimp connectors made the connections easy. The hardest part was wiring up the backup camera. I had to find the wire to my reverse lights in a plug in the passenger foot rest and similarly I powered the backup camera by splicing into my backup light wire. That works fine, though the picture flickers occasionally. I suspect that's the wiring/ power and not a camera issue.

Sound quality was fine while it lasted. It does cut out the first second of each song when listening to my iPhone over Bluetooth, but that was only a minor annoyance. The touch screen interface worked fine for me. The interface isn't super intuitive but the icons are nice and big and the screen sensitivity was fine. It was great value for the money for the 3 months that it worked.
text_fidelity_b: BOSS Audio Systems B9351WRC Double Din, Touchscreen, Bluetooth, DVD CD MP3 USB SD AM FM Car Stereo, 6.2 Inch Digital LCD Monitor, Wireless Remote, Wireless Rear License Plate Camera.

text_fidelity_a:
SABRENT Rocket Q 500GB NVMe PCIe M.2 2280 Internal SSD High Performance Solid State Drive R/W 2000/1000MB/s (SB-RKTQ-500) Compared to the Crucial 1TB M2 NVME I reviewed earlier, this Sabrent 512GB model benchmarks a little faster. And it works just fine on a PCI M2 adapter card, which are only a few bucks. (I bought the cheapest one available and it works.)

The NVME still offers much faster R/W speeds than other drives even when used with SATA 1 (as on my workstation). For example, the SSD I was using as my hard disk benchmarks at about 220MB/second. The Sabrent NVME on a PCI card benchmarks at about 1.5GB/second.

This time I experimented to see if I could get Debian Linux distro running on the NVME on my older workstation.

It took a few tries. Getting the OS to boot directly from the NVME was a no-go. Since the NVME is mounted on an adapter card, I had hoped it would trick the system into thinking it was just an ordinary SATA drive and boot from it. But that didn't happen.

So what I did was installed all the Linux OS EXCEPT for the boot folder on the NVME, and put the boot folder on the SSD HDD. So it boots from the SSD but the entire OS is on the NVME and runs from it.

Step one:

The partition manager in the Debian installer didn't want to partition the NVME at first.

So I bailed out of it and used GParted (Gnome disks utility couldn't do this) to "create partition table" and selected msdos as type. That wiped everything and turned the whole drive into unallocated space. From that point the partition manager worked.

Step two:

From the linux bootable USB installer I partitioned the SSD (not the NVME) with a primary partition labeled (to be mounted) as /boot. (You can make this partition most any size from a few GB on up---the boot files don't require a lot of space.) The remaining space I manually labeled as /msc.

I partitioned the NVME so the installer would put everything else on it, starting with / (root). You can simply make the whole NVME / root and the installer will take care of putting everything else on that drive, or you can do what I did and set up size-defined partitions for /home, /usr, and so on.

After installing the system, the installer asks where you want the bootloader GRUB installed. I selected the SSD.

It worked. The SSD does the booting to the NVME, which then runs the OS. And it did improve speed.
text_fidelity_b: SABRENT Rocket Q 500GB NVMe PCIe M.2 2280 Internal SSD High Performance Solid State Drive R/W 2000/1000MB/s (SB-RKTQ-500)

text_fidelity_a:
Magellan Crossover 3.5-Inch Portable GPS Navigator OK, so I can't compare the performance of this GPS system to any other as this was the first time I've ever used or needed something like this. But I read a lot of reviews, and I do mean a lot of them, for a couple of weeks before making my decision and I'm pleased that for a first experience I purchased a Magellan Crossover.

Let me explain, I work in sales. I travel to a lot of large towns/ small cities in my territory that are in Arkansas. I had never been to these towns before. Apparently, the city leaders do not care if one can find their way around them because most of them have terrible city maps available and/or do not bother to put street signs up. This made it a challenge to find my customers even with a map.

So the idea of a GPS came to mind and I took the plunge. This little unit worked exactly the way I wanted for 2 days then stopped working half way through the second day. Not even pressing the reset button helped. (sigh) I called the people I purchased it from and they paid to have it Fed-Exed back to them for replacement. Apparently I got a defective model. Hey, it happens to all of us. So by the end of this week I'll have my replacement and will be ready to roll again.

This was a great time saver for me. I would get to a town, input the first address and it would get me to my first stop. When I was done there I would input the next address and it accurately got me to the next place I needed to be. It literally saved me a couple hours a day in wasted travel time by my not having to stop, get directions from a local (that were usually wrong) and repeating that process over and over.

The screen was bright and easy to read, the voice plenty loud enough. And the unit was easy learn to use. I gave it 5 stars for performance. I can't really fault the manufacturer for a faulty unit. Those things are hard to predict and usually are few and far between.

So, unless the next unit is also defective, at which time I will then have to reconsider and write a more negative review LOL, this little GPS unit is a great buy for a first time user.

[...].
text_fidelity_b: Magellan Crossover 3.5-Inch Portable GPS Navigator

And even then, parts of the data are missing. For example it may say I only walked a few feet a certain day, when I actually walked many miles. The vivoifit2 will have the correct amount, but it never sends the right data to the software any longer.

Actually really loved this item when I first got it. It worked great - accurately counting my steps. Wearing it made me push myself to walk further each day and also made me mindful of eating healthier. It used to sync fast and correctly.

I wore this kayaking - which I do several times a week and found it to be totally waterproof.

Sleep feature nice, but I don't really need that data.

The plastic band is a bit sweaty. I wore it super lose because of this. Even so, I bit uncomfortable to always have a perspiring wrist. I ordered the silver watch band, but after three weeks it still hadn't even shipped out. Glad it didn't since the Vivofit2 no longer works.

So in short, if it is OK that it only functions a few weeks, then this is wonderful item.But, if you plan to use for a longer period of time, this is not good.

text_fidelity_a:
Echo Dot (2nd Generation) - Smart speaker with Alexa - White Great price and fun to play with. If you're interested in smart home technology this is a great place to start since it's easy to use and connect to other devices down the road. I bought several as Christmas gifts and when people figured out how to use it they loved it. The built in speaker is ok, I knew it wasn't as good as the more expensive Echo so I wasn't disappointed. If you already have a Bluetooth speaker or sound quality isn't a huge factor for you out of the box then you can't beat the price. I don't have any issues hearing Alexa's responses with the built in speaker, but when I want to listen to music I just connect my Bluetooth speaker (very easy to do) and can move it around the house with no problems. We have a dot on each floor of our house (2 stories) that are located in the most used areas. I keep a Bluetooth speaker in our bedroom and use the Alexa remote to interact with the Dot in our tv room since she can't hear me as well. This allows you to still connect to, and hear Alexa, without having to yell and strain to hear her.

The shopping list and to do list feature I really like since I'm horrible at writing down what we need around the house before I go shopping. I just tell her what to add to my list as I notice it, and it instantly shows up in the Alexa app which I can open when I get to the store and add/delete items. I also love these features to capture random things I want to research later like book titles, tv shows, serial numbers for parts etc that I might forget if I don't have it written down somewhere.

The only reason I didn't give the dot 5 stars is because most of the skills that are available right now leave a lot to be desired. I'm sure down the road this will improve but there isn't a lot to choose from right now that has a lot of practical use. Like a lot of people I would prefer Alexa be able to answer questions based on a Google search rather than having to enable skills for different things. If I want to know what flu symptons are she doesn't understand what I'm asking. But when you factor in everything she can do, and what she can connect with, then the dot is definitely still worth purchasing based on the price.
text_fidelity_b: Echo Dot (2nd Generation) - Smart speaker with Alexa - White

Bestlight 48 LED Macro Ring Light With 6 Adaptors Rings for Canon Digital EOS Rebel SL1 (100D),T5i(700D),T4i(650D),T3(1100D),T3i(600D),60D,60Da,50D,Nikon D5300,D5000,D3000,D3200,D5100 DSLR Cameras 48 LED unit - (since several items are listed under one product ID)
Positives:
- It is what it looks like, does what it claims to do, and basically works
- cheap
- comes with an AC adapter!! Wow. You can pay a lot for a light that doesn't

Negatives: I'm using this for Macro work (I'm new to macro) so that's the perspective I'm coming from
- Not Bright Enough! It's just not all that bright. Not enough to light a subject by itself for macro purposes. I doubt it's adequate for more than a highlight for portraiture. This is why 2 stars. If a light doesn't light - it's not a light.

Really that's it. This is not a knock to the light (and not why I gave it a low rating), but if you are planning on using it for macro, buy a flash instead. A flash will not only have higher output, but will help freeze the camera shake (a big macro problem). Also, I thought the full time light would be better for live insects (you can see what you're doing!), but it's the opposite. You need the flash to freeze action. Not a criticism (this light does not advertise itself as a flash), but something to know.

UPDATE: I used it a couple more times. I am finding it more useful than initially when very close in. I would still strongly recommend a flash for this unless you have a compelling reason for continuous illumination (e.g you're waiting for a bug to crawl into frame and it's too dark to see otherwise. Though the lights would probably scare the bug). If you have a pretty solid tripod setup, this can work for longer exposure macro. Not great though. Upped to 3 stars.
text_fidelity_b: Bestlight 48 LED Macro Ring Light With 6 Adaptors Rings for Canon Digital EOS Rebel SL1 (100D),T5i(700D),T4i(650D),T3(1100D),T3i(600D),60D,60Da,50D,Nikon D5300,D5000,D3000,D3200,D5100 DSLR Cameras

And I guess the Christmas-tree tips are a bit different because so far these headphones are the only one that have not leaked, but I do have to insert them deep into ear canal. I use them in my Endless Pool, so I don't know how they will perform in regular pool during turns and flips, but my guess is because of their lightness they will work fine. text_fidelity_a:
Verso Prologue Case Cover for Kindle Fire, Tan (does not fit Kindle Fire HD) At first glance, this appears to be an elegant folio cover for tablets; it has an authentic-looking antique book design with embossing on the faux leather, some "gold" leafing, and real top-stitching, and it fits nicely on a book shelf (great disguise if you think you need to hide your device for whatever reason). While the design is lovely and the black microfiber supposedly prevents your screen from getting scratched, the way the tablet is held in is by four elastic straps that do an ok job, but I feel in time will wear out. Because of that concern, the design gets 4/5 stars

The function of this folio is to give the tablet a different look and ease of portability without fear of it breaking. It also helps serve as a dust cover for those who have tablets that don't always use them. This is not made for all terrain, though it's good and light weight enough for public transport. Parks and other minor recreational places are ok. I wouldn't take this folio camping or to the beach do to fear of destroying both the folio and tablet. Even though there is a cover there is a minor opening that doesn't really stay closed with the tablet in it. This folio doesn't really appear to protect a tablet from accidental drops. For every day use, this gets a 3.5/5, and for not-so every day use (rougher environments), it's closer to 1/5, so bear that in mind when deciding what case to buy.

The positive thing about this folio is that it fits most 7.1 inch tablets It did fit the Galaxy Tab 7.1 and the original kindle with keyboard. I would recommend an accessories pack to go along with the folio, since screen protector is a must! Over all for a folio I would give it 3.5/5 rounded up to 4. While is is beautiful, it only keeps to the basics of what a tablet user needs.
text_fidelity_b: Verso Prologue Case Cover for Kindle Fire, Tan (does not fit Kindle Fire HD)

text_fidelity_a:
Koss 155524 UR40 Collapsible Over-Ear Headphones ...and after 13 years of heavy use, I was curious... here's my old headphones!

I went looking, because I like them so much all this time!

A couple things.

The mesh head thing- it only stayed on a couple years. They headphones worked better without it anyhow I think. Smoother on my hair. Which has a fine texture, and is a bit frizzy- lots of fine short pieces. Sometimes the foldable joints catch in them. This happens on earrings, necklaces, other headphones and other things as well. No more on this product really. Function of having fine curly hair.

Sound has always been fantastic. I love the sound and am sad when I send a ton of cash on headphones that don't come close.

They are not a snug fit, but, are soft enough and comfy enough to wear to bed. Because of the tender fabric, it's started to deteriorate on the smooth fake leathery bits. So so soft all this time though. Really to last 13 years, NO COMPLAINTS!!!.

Not snug enough to work out in. Snug enough to casually hike or walk in. They won't just fall right off or anything.

Lightweight. Easy to make a pouch or toss them into a ziplock freezer quart bag to travel and keep them in your pack or bag more tidily.

I would agree with most reviews. I tend to consider the cables 'supple' instead of 'flimsy'-- and this is an important difference! Supple cables don't just out at awkward angles and get caught on as much stuff. You can keep your music device in your pocket and the cable stays nicely under your coat or shirt and bends where you need it to stay and likes being there rather than tugging intself back in to the shape it wants to be in like a stiffer cable.

These are one of the few products I would give 10 stars to if I could.

And I still would after 13 years!!!!!!

Oh,

Actually they still work fine too. Really. I just noticed they are really a little fiddly nowadays because I used them so much, and was wondering if they still made them.

It's a bit disturbing that amazon remembered I bought them so long ago, though. I'm starting to hope Amazon never holds a grudge against me, cause they never forget!!
text_fidelity_b: Koss 155524 UR40 Collapsible Over-Ear Headphones

Canon EF 100mm f/2.8 Macro USM Fixed Lens for Canon SLR Cameras Although this lens is intended for macro photography, it's also a great lens for general purpose shots, or portrait shots. The lens produces beautiful sharp images and is a fast, accurate focuser. The lens is moderately heavy and bulky, so I wouldn't classify it as eminently carryable, and without image stabilization, you might suffer hand shake blur if you're not shooting at the wide end; at smaller apertures, using it with a tripod is highly recommended. But if you're buying it primarily to get into macro this shouldn't much matter as tripod shooting with macro is virtually a necessity, and completely expected.

The 100mm focal length is a nice compromise when you want to get close to small subjects (particularly insects) but are limited to how close you can get before scaring the subject off - as a comparison with the 180mm macro, you would want to factor in a consideration as to what you might like to shoot most of the time - big spiders that you'd rather stay well away from might be an application more suited to the 180mm, for instance, but if you are keen to shoot mostly flowers, the 180 might be more length than you really need.

In short, the 100mm macro is one of my "keeper" lenses, a real performer.
text_fidelity_b: Canon EF 100mm f/2.8 Macro USM Fixed Lens for Canon SLR Cameras

Jaybird X4 Wireless Bluetooth Headphones for Sport Fitness and Running, Compatible with iOS and Android Smartphones: Sweatproof and Waterproof - Black Metallic/Flash These are very good Bluetooth earbuds for sports use. Construction is very lightweight, but still very durable. Earpieces are very secure when I'm running or working out at the gym and more than comfortable enough for hour-long workouts. Sound quality is pretty good out-of-the-box, but a little thin at the higher frequencies (especially noticeable with acoustic music). Fortunately, Jaybird has a great smartphone app you can use to equalize the sound. I was never very good at designing my own equalization profiles by ear, but the app has several ready made profiles so I just picked the one that sounded best with my favorite music (boosting higher frequencies more than lower frequencies). There is no noise cancellation, but noise isolation is very good with the included foam eartips (not the default eartips).

I really do not like that you need a special dongle to recharge this headset. You can't just plug a standard USB cable directly into these, like with most Bluetooth headset. This may have something to do with the headset's waterproof rating, but other headsets I own are also waterproof and can still be recharged with a standard cable. I am concerned that the proprietary charging dongle will get lost or broken or I will just forget to bring it with me when traveling.
text_fidelity_b: Jaybird X4 Wireless Bluetooth Headphones for Sport Fitness and Running, Compatible with iOS and Android Smartphones: Sweatproof and Waterproof - Black Metallic/Flash

text_fidelity_a:
woednx Smart Watch,1.4''Full Touch Fitness Tracker with Heart Rate,Blood Pressure and Sleep Monitor,Message Notification,Smartwatch for Men WomenIP68 Waterproof Smartwatch Sports for iOS Android-Blue PROS

1. The silicone band is very comfortable. Apparently if it breaks, it can be replaced, though I’m not sure where or how you would buy a new band.

2. The appearance is sleek and modern, and the size of the watch face makes the digital numbers easy to read.

3. It has a rechargeable battery, which may have a longer life than the non-rechargeable batteries of most sports watches.

4. If you want a smart watch that is far cheaper than most brands, this might work for you.

CONS

1. There are three primary functions that I use a sports watch for: to instantly check the time, a stopwatch, and a timer. It irritated me no end with this watch that, after only a few seconds of being lit up, its face goes dark. While this might save the charge on the rechargeable battery, there are plenty of times when my right hand it not free to punch the button on this watch to light up its face, and I can’t quickly and conveniently check the time! It is also a hassle trying to use the stopwatch and timer functions.

2. I absolutely loathe the way this watch’s battery is recharged. Instead of using a standard C cable, the charging cable attaches magnetically, and it becomes detached far too easily. There is also no warning when the battery of this watch is about to go dead.

3. I don’t like the software this phone uses. It is a major hassle to learn for what I personally consider very little useful return. Why? Because most of the functions offered by this watch that are of any interest to me I can get through my smartphone. I use my phone and a Bluetooth for phone calls, texting, music, and hearing alarms. I check the weather by looking around me when outside or looking at weather apps on my phone. I use my phone for photography.
The rest of the functions this watch offers I personally find to be useless. I do not need a watch to tell me how to do a deep breathing exercises. As a healthy individual with no heart issues, I do not need to monitor my heart rate 24/7. (And if I did, I would use medical equipment that is far more reliable than this cheap watch.) I don’t need to obsessively monitor my sleep. (And, again, if I did, I wouldn’t trust this cheap watch to do an accurate job of it.)

4. Its pedometer function might have been of use to me, but unfortunately, it is inaccurate.

CONCLUSION

I dumped this watch and went back to a regular, inexpensive sports watch.

text_fidelity_a:
Bose Companion 20 Multimedia Speaker System Silver I wanted a set of speakers to use mainly for my Kindle Fire and MP3 player, but also as my computer speakers. Due to space constraints, a 2.0 system was my only option, since a subwoofer (regardless of the size) would be problematic.

So the search began. There were several speakers that sounded great, including the Creative Gigaworks, M Audio and Audioengine. However, they lacked the convenience features I wanted such as ease of connecting/disconnecting a tablet and volume control without having to reach out and touch the speaker.

The Bose Companion 20 initially caught my eye because of the control pod. That was a great solution to my problems since I could control the volume right on my desk plus have the ability to plug in/unplug a tablet very easily. The sound quality sealed the deal - everyone who hears these speakers think they are a 2.1 set due to the ample bass. But, the bass is not at the expense of clear mid and upper ranges.

I use these 60% for music and 40% for video, and for both applications, the sound quality has been just wonderful. I'm also impressed that they sound just as good with the volume dialed way down as they do at moderate or blast-out-the-walls loud.

The control pod is very well made. It has a nice weight to it and a non-skid backing so it stays put. The volume control works very smoothly with a solid feel. I'm especially fond of being able to turn the speakers on and off by just touching the control pod.

You can connect it to the PC and to an aux device (such as a tablet) and use both at the same time. That's important since I want to listen to music or a video from my Fire, but still want to hear a chime when an email arrives.

My complaints are that the control pod cable is a bit too short for my needs. It's about 5 foot long, which is ample if you have the speakers next to your PC, but I have my speakers on a shelf above my desk. I was able to arrange things to make it work, but another foot or two of cable (or the ability to purchase an extension) would have been nice. It's a custom cable, so an off-the-shelf extension is not possible.

My other complaint is the price. I was able to get a used pair for half of the regular price. I think these are a bit overpriced at the regular price. But, Bose hit a really unique niche - the ability to have great sound without any compromise in convenience. If you want both, there's a high cost for admission.

If the price is not an issue, these very much deserve a hard look if you're in the market for a great sounding pair of 2.0 speakers. Highly recommend.
text_fidelity_b: Bose Companion 20 Multimedia Speaker System Silver

Garmin Friction Mount This is a highly quality well built item, and will hold in place well, but will not work for me.

First off, this is bigger than I imagined and it has a commanding presence on your dash. The rubber part is a lint collector so looks terrible against a nice black dash. The black pad and black mount are a green black and a purple black. The plastic riser mount itself was significantly less flexible than I needed, I basically could not get the Garmin to point in the direction I wanted no matter how I placed the rubber pad, because the mount does not swivel left and right at all and has fixed limits to the side. Then, the mount raises up higher than I wanted, more or less blocked good site lines. The adhesive definitely removes whatever is on your dash (vinyl protectant) on removal and leaves something behind, but it's not damaging the dash and I suspect it will clean up. The rubber base will conform to whatever shape, but it was really difficult to get a nice flush mount, because to test and form it requires a number of trials, and I had already removed the adhesive backing (no instructions)... NOTE for users, shape and place thoroughly before removing the backing.

Ultimately, this product probably does what it's intended to do if you know exactly what it is, I need something more low profile and flexible.
text_fidelity_b: Garmin Friction Mount

text_fidelity_a:
Kindle Fire (Previous Generation - 1st) The Fire and I have been inseparable since its arrival. I love this tablet! The professional reviews I'd read before I received it set my expectations pretty low by saying it's a nice device for the price, but the reality is that it's just a really nice device!

I have an iPad (first generation..., so no camera), and I like it, but I'm not a power iPad user. I use it to stream movies, read, surf the internet, and play games. The Kindle Fire does all of those things, but has the added bonus of being more portable, which is a pretty big deal to me. My iPad has always been a home device for me because it's too big to realistically throw in my purse. The Fire is the perfect size for portability! However, it is still significantly larger than a smartphone, so I can read or watch movies without squinting or holding a device up to my face.

One big weakness it does have - the E-Ink on the other Kindle models is far easier on the eyes when doing heavy reading. I'm hanging on to my Kindle 3 for that reason. The kind of reading I'll be doing on my Fire is more along the lines of magazine reading, looking at recipes, newspaper articles, stuff like that.

Overall, the Fire is a solid purchase. If you're thinking about buying it, just do it. You won't be disappointed!
text_fidelity_b: Kindle Fire (Previous Generation - 1st)

SABRENT 4TB Rocket NVMe PCIe M.2 2280 Internal SSD High Performance Solid State Drive (SB-ROCKET-4TB) I tested this in a USB 3 adapter on my MacBook Air. Why would I do that? What could possibly be the point?

Well, I couldn't persuade my son to pull his m.2 drive and test this one against it (haven't yet, anyway - next time he wants a favor bad enough to stop playing Dark Souls to as me for it, I will update with results).

text_fidelity_a:
Fitbit Versa Smart Watch, Peach/Rose Gold Aluminium, One Size (S & L Bands Included), Heart Rate Monitor This little device does a lot.
While it is sort of a smart watch, it sort of isn't, too. But what it does, it does well.

The good:
- Excellent selection of watch faces, including cute, clever, big, pretty, etc. You can change your face every day to match your clothes if you want.
- If I understand correctly, you can use it with other services, like Spark People.
- measures pulse, steps, miles. Tracks exercise on demand.
- motivates in numerous ways. Reminders to stand up, encouragement to finish your goal steps for the hour, challenges, even "travel" challenges that are longer term.
- large userbase. You can network with more of your friends on Fitbit than on any other fitness watch.
- big face without losing attractiveness
- large variety of replacement bands available from third parties, some very pretty.
- Can be used with many other fitness applications.
- Detects sleep surprisingly accurately
- Lots of settings options
- A decent number of apps available
- Handles the shower well
- If you never have to take it off except to charge, it's harder to lose it.
- Charges very quickly
- The charger is an awesome design and easy to use
- You can always have your alarms with you so you never miss them.

The irritating
- All changes have to be made through the app.
- If you don't sync often enough, it loses your data
- Sync can take a long time.
- The battery life is considerably shorter than I expected. It's about 2 1/2 days if I have constant sync turned off.
- Don't even bother with constant sync unless you're willing to take it off to charge a lot.
- All the music apps are paid

All in all, though, the pros are big and the cons are small. Enough that it still warrants a 5 star review.
text_fidelity_b: Fitbit Versa Smart Watch, Peach/Rose Gold Aluminium, One Size (S & L Bands Included), Heart Rate Monitor

text_fidelity_a:
AMD FD8350FRHKBOX FX-8350 FX-Series 8-Core Black Edition Processor Immediately after installing I noticed the idle speed just sitting in BIOS to be 50C. That's quite a bit! More than any processor I've come across.
At first I thought I seated it wrong so I undid the heat sink, used really good thermal paste and tried once more.
Same result. Idle temp at 50C.
And under load it's getting up to into the low 60s and termal throttling like crazy. However it seems to perform well even under that heavy load, which is nice if that's all you care about.
But I'm doing a build for my dad and I don't think he'd be content with having to hear a jet engine under his desk day in and day out. So I'm going to have to look elsewhere.
That's on me though. I probably should have known better from my experience with another FX processor. Ah well.
Still considering if I'm returning this or not.

UPDATE:
Ok, I did some more digging and it sounds like my motherboard is not equipped to handle this processor.
WARNING: If you have a MSI 970A-G46 Motherboard DO NOT BUY THIS PROCESSOR.
Go research "MSI 970A-G46 FX 8350"
You'll find numerous testimonials of people who have had terminal issues trying to use a FX 8350 with this board.
Since the MB is at fault for this and I can not accurately benchmark this product, I'll give AMD the benefit of the doubt and make this 5 stars.
text_fidelity_b: AMD FD8350FRHKBOX FX-8350 FX-Series 8-Core Black Edition Processor

text_fidelity_a:
JVC Soft Wireless Earbud with Stayfit Tips, Remote and Mic and Bluetooth Violet (HA-FX9BTV) 3.5 stars taking price into account

With headphones, it is always a blend of "you get what you paid for", and comparing to others at a similar price point.
How do these compare? Well, they are about average for the $20-$40 range. Not much better, not much worse. And as is the case with headphones, for a bit more, you can do MUCH better, and for a bit less, you will get roughly similar results. (In other words, headphones under $75-$100 are, more or less very similar, and then suddenly, your options get drastically better.)

Here's my analysis on the general sound quality and other features:

MISC:
Phone calls: 5 stars: Easy to use, works great for calls on both ends, and blocks outside sound quite well!
Ease of use/pairing: 5 stars: It passed the test of not having to read instructions, meaning it is incredibly simple to pair and use
Appearance: 5 stars: Neat! It's colorful and fun, as well as practical and functional!
External noise: 4 stars: Because it has a pretty tight seal, it is like an earplug, blocking outside sound quite effectively
Comfort: 3 stars: comparable to others of this design. Totally fine at first, and annoying after long use.

SOUND:
Treble: 2 stars: quite tinny
Bass: 2 stars: ok depth, not great, not very powerful
Overall: 2 stars: not much detail in the sound, but it can get pretty loud without distorting, and it is definitely good enough for basic listening and phone calls. There also appears to be a *very slight* hiss in quiet/silent moments when the volume is louder.

OVERALL:
The average is 28 out of 40 possible points, or 70% (a "C" grade, if it were going to school ;-), but because the above analysis does not take price point into account, comparing this to brands like Bose, as well as dollar store headphones, this means that for the current list price of roughly $29.99, this is a reasonable expectation.

The average number of stars based on my rubric is 3.5 stars: decent for this price point, and certainly good enough to enjoy music and spoken word, and to have successful phone calls.
text_fidelity_b: JVC Soft Wireless Earbud with Stayfit Tips, Remote and Mic and Bluetooth Violet (HA-FX9BTV)

text_fidelity_a:
CPR V5000 Call Blocker for Landline Phones – Stop All Unwanted Calls at a Touch of a Button - Join Over 1 Million Satisfied Customers This is my second review, because I just had to buy a second unit, thanks to my honored telephone/wireless provider. Loved the first one I bought and considered it indispensable. Then Cox decided to change all its landline customers to VoIP. I asked the Cox tech to install it on the gigantic space-gobbling, dust-collecting modem he deposited on my desk, and he said Cox wouldn’t touch anything that wasn’t Cox equipment. Besides, said he, it wouldn’t work with the new equipment, anyway. (This assessment, it develops, was...uhm...in error).

Cox was offering NoMoRobo to its new VoIP customers, and having seen good reviews of that service, I figured it would substitute for the CPR Call Blocker. Because I expected I couldn't figure out how to attach CPR gadgetry to the accursed modem, I donated the now supposedly unusable device.

Mistake.

NoMoRobo turned out to be an endlessly annoying bust. To block a call from a phone number, NoMoRobo has to let the first jangle ring through. This is how it identifies fake phone numbers. Unlike the CPR 5000, it apparently has no preprogrammed numbers; thus every pest's nuisance call just comes right through. And unlike the CPR v5000, it seems unable to identify rogue VoIP/IP rogue diallers, leaving you vulnerable to an expensive scam.

I do technical editing for scientists and mathematicians whose first language is not English. This work requires sustained, close attention. It is not facilitated by constant interruptions. So NoMoRobo's first-ring technology was a deal-killer from the git-go.

Then we have the problem that you can’t signal NoMoRobo that a number is bad with a push of a button. You have to go online to their Website and fill out a freaking form! You have to retrieve the offending number from your phone’s memory, type it into the form, report the caller’s name, say what time the call occurred…all of which adds the insult of time suck to the injury of phone scamming. As hoop-jumps go, it’s brain-banging pointless: the robocallers simply generate new numbers, potentially dialing you from every telephone number in your exchange. Or, for that matter, in any exchange.

With the CPR Call Blocker, if you’re on a cordless extension, you simply press the “Talk” button and then press #2; if you’re at your desk where the device is sitting, you don’t even have to pick up. Just reach over and press that big red “BLOCK” button.

The highly satisfying big red BLOCK button….

Normally I get at least a dozen nuisance robocalls a day, starting at 8 a.m. (or earlier) and running through till 8 or 9 p.m. That's a bare minimum. Yesterday I attached the new CPR unit to the phone system, fairly early in the afternoon. This task, BTW, proved to be *vastly* easier than I imagined it would be. Once the device was online, NOT EVEN ONE MORE NUISANCE CALL got through! Feeling suspicious, I dialed the landline number from my cell phone: it rang right through. That suggests the thing blocked four to six robocalls. Right now it's about 10 the next morning, and so far just one call has managed to get past the CPR device.
text_fidelity_b: CPR V5000 Call Blocker for Landline Phones – Stop All Unwanted Calls at a Touch of a Button - Join Over 1 Million Satisfied Customers

text_fidelity_a:
Apple 2020 iPad Air (10.9-inch, Wi-Fi + Cellular, 64GB) - Green (4th Generation) Or, at least, a laptop go away until I can afford a better laptop-er.

So far, this is not that. For one thing, the expensive keyboard case has amazing keys, but in a tiny little format that isn't really easy to type on quickly, if you are used to using all of both of your hands. The action is way better than my laptop's, but it's cramped.

Having a trackpad is lovely. It was what I had been waiting for before upgrading from my gen1 iPad Air. But the case again interferes with functionality because you can't really adjust the iPad angle. The iPad itself is sleek and gorgeous. And it's a lot faster than my old iPad. And it has a lot more space in it. And - in theory - it should run app versions of everything I use my laptop for.

In theory.

And it almost does.

Kind of.

But it's a pain and a half to set up. Its security features won't let it transfer passwords from my other devices, which means that all of those passwords I let Apple suggest for me (before I learned the hard way that Apple doesn't always save them after setting them) - I have to enter by hand on the iPad. Mind you, I got the iPad's settings from a backup of a different iPad that had all those passwords already. Anyway, I can't even think of getting rid of my laptop, because I need it to look up my passwords so that I can enter them on the iPad.

(Yes, I know it's supposed to be as easy at turning on the keychain. It's not, though.)

Bottom lines? Yes, it's pretty and fast. No, it's not worth the money, and I wouldn't buy it again (I would either get a mini to do phone games and quick emails or shell out for the big iPad Pro and be done with laptops forever once I got my passwords in that one). Yes, I'm keeping it and am open to changing my mind.

Fitbit One Wireless Activity Plus Sleep Tracker, Black Three things have changed my life! FITBIT, Walking Workouts and Walking 4 Fun.

FITBIT ONE - I have been faithfully wearing it. Using the calories in and out featured on the app. It has a safety leash and I wear it attached to my bra. I do a Jessica Smith DVD - 10K Walking Workout (see link on bottom of this review) and Leslie Sansone ("Walk at Home"). However, ONE is super accurate on my walks outside and around the office. My bottom line is 10K steps a day but I tend to walk 17K a day. I worked my way up to this since October 2015. I have a sedentary job so walking happens 3 to 4 times a day with a minimum of a mile on each walk. Yes, I have lost weight, @ 40 lbs. There is at least that much more that needs to be lost as well. Hair color is silver if that helps you define the situation.

I love the little activity record feature and use it often (hold down the button to start and hold it down to end when activity is over). This is great when competing with friends where a challenge is inevitable. Speaking of friends. YEAH! That is where the FITBITs excel. I have a few friends in my community now and I love keeping up with them. Motivation features are fantastic!

This little baby doesn't buzz, which also means that the battery life is HUGE!! I think it goes 7 to 8 days before I need to be charged up. I tend to let it go dead because it warns you it needs to be charged about 1 1/2 days before it really does. I've only charged mine 3x now. It takes about an hour to charge. I wait until the visible battery = FULL!

This sweet little tracker is awesome! I started test driving the flex before getting the ONE which I also enjoyed but not as much as this one. I will buy the HR when this ONE dies or I just feel like bringing home another one. The reason I like this one better than the flex is because I don't tend to be an arm swinger and for me this one seems to work better (walking while pushing a cart). The best thing about the arm band models is that you affix it and forget it (until charging time) for which you should get a phone alert.

I don't bother with the sleep feature because I have an app (Sleep Cycle Alarm) on the phone that I use for which I love the beautiful melodious wake up sound. However the ONE comes with a little band for you to slide the ONE into obtain the reading for sleep.

text_fidelity_a:
VIZIO Sound Bar for TV, 28” 2.1 Surround Sound System for TV with Wireless Subwoofer and Bluetooth, Channel Home Theater Sound Bar – Remote SB2821-D6 The first delivery had subwoofer that was dead on arrival. No power.

They sent a replacement. It works great. Music streaming from my phone or computer by bluetooth sounds great. Better than my Bose.

If you want instruction on how to operate this thing properly look at the copied review below. This was helpful.

One other or two were somewhat helpful.

The instructions they put in the package gets the thing on but doesn't tell you how to operate it.

FYI:

"Please handle this unit with care when taking it out of the box. The sub-woofer in particular, which has the speaker cone located on the bottom of the sub-woofer. If you grab it from the bottom, you could damage it very easily. When set up properly, I found this Sound Bar to have very good sound. However it did take me awhile to reach this state. Because like most men, I know everything, I skipped through the instructions, plugged in the sound bar and was extremely disappointed in the quality of the sound. Here are a few tips to make things easier. If you're doing a horizontal installation in front of the TV at ear level, the sound button the the bar should be located on top, and the small lights that show volume level, etc., should be located on the left when facing your TV. That way the speakers are facing you. Also, I had a difficult time finding the audio settings on my TV to turn off the internal speakers and use the external speakers. Naturally I thought, heck just turn down the volume on the TV speakers to zero and it should be the same thing. Wrong !! You have to find and turn on the external speakers, and turn off the internal speakers for this sound bar to work properly. The sound bar does come with a remote, which is an absolute necessity no matter which sound bar you order. Read the instruction manual carefully, as you have to use the 'previous" and "next" buttons to adjust the Sub-woofer, Bass and Treble settings. Since I know everything, I naturally assumed the volume up and down buttons would adjust these settings. Wrong !! Also, there are buttons to enable TruVolume, and TruSurround HD, but the manual doesn't clarify exactly when to use these settings or what they actually do. I suggest trying both settings and see if you notice any difference in sound quality. I've read a few complaints about the bass not being that strong, but I found it to be excellent. I wonder if these users had the sub-woofer in the correct location, and if they figured out how to raise the sub-woofer level using the remote, and if the sub-woofer stopped working and needed to be "re-linked". I had to re-link mine, and although the instructions could be better, got the sub-woofer working properly in a few minutes. With the sub-woofer is turned on, located in the right area, and adjusted with the remote, you should be very happy with the results. Why only 4 stars for this product? First, the instruction manual could have been more informative about the settings on the remote, and second the ergonomics of the remote are in my opinion very bad. The volume adjustment in particular is usually an up and down toggle on every remote I ever used, but not on this one. The technical designer genius of this remote decided to put a big square "enter/play/pause button between the up and down volume adjustment buttons. Hence adjusting the volume by feel is the worst of any remote I've ever had. That being said, once set up properly, you should be extremely happy with the sound quality of this sound bar."
text_fidelity_b: VIZIO Sound Bar for TV, 28” 2.1 Surround Sound System for TV with Wireless Subwoofer and Bluetooth, Channel Home Theater Sound Bar – Remote SB2821-D6

text_fidelity_a:
Ring Video Doorbell 2 with HD Video, Motion Activated Alerts, Easy Installation called due to battery not charging although we spent the money to hard wire it..... and got an email from them. box says it works to -5F. this is what the email states..... Important temperatures

The following are key temperatures to watch out for in regards to your batteries.

36°F (3°C): The battery may not hold a charge as effectively, resulting in you having to charge the unit more frequently.
32°F (0°C): The battery may not charge at all. Even hardwired configurations may not charge the battery.
-5°F (-20.5°C): The battery may stop working completely until temperatures warm up.
What to do when it gets cold

Bring your device inside: When it gets cold and your device's battery runs out, bring your entire device inside and charge the battery with a USB cord. This will allow your device to warm up while the battery charges.
Make sure your battery is charged to 100%: When charging your battery, be sure that it reaches 100% before your remount the device. While the battery still won't be as effective as when the temperatures are warmer, making sure that the battery is at 100% will allow your device to work as long as possible.
Monitor your charge and the temperature: As long as the temperature hovers around the points listed above, you may have issues with battery charge. Therefore it's important to constantly monitor your battery life when it gets cold to make sure your device is always working.
text_fidelity_b: Ring Video Doorbell 2 with HD Video, Motion Activated Alerts, Easy Installation

text_fidelity_a:
Plantronics 211856-99 Backbeat Fit 3100 True Wireless Earbuds, Sweatproof and Waterproof In Ear Workout Headphones, Grey There are "true wireless" earbuds on Amazon for half of this price, but I have tried several of them and they all suffer from poor-to-mediocre sound quality as well as poor battery life. These Plantronics earbuds cost more, but they have great sound quality as well as great battery life. I hear a good amount of bass as well as good clarity in the higher frequencies. My favorite music sounds muddy on cheaper wireless earbuds, but sounds great on these. 5 hour battery life per charge is almost double what the cheap earbuds give me. The ear hooks look clunky, but they are very comfortable and never fall off when I'm jogging or working out.

As with all "true wireless" earbuds, you have to control them with a series of short and long taps on the sides of the earbuds (to change volume, skip around in your music, answer phone calls, etc). If you have a hard time remembering all those commands (as I do), you can always pull out your phone and do the same thing from there.

If you cannot afford "true wireless" earbuds at this price level, my advice is to forget the "true wireless" design and look at Bluetooth earbuds that have a wire connecting the two sides. That style is slightly uglier than "true wireless" but has much better battery life and sound quality for similar price levels and there are pretty good products for much cheaper prices than the "true wireless" design.

I see some review complaints about connectivity and charging problems. My earbuds have worked perfectly with no dropouts, etc. As with any electronic gadget, there is always the possibility of a manufacturing flaw. I would definitely return a product that did not work flawlessly.

Note that this particular Plantronics model is not noise-cancelling or noise-isolating. You will hear some background noise, which is safer if you use them when walking or working in a busy environment. Plantronics does sell noise cancelling earbuds that you could choose instead if that feature is useful and important to you.
text_fidelity_b: Plantronics 211856-99 Backbeat Fit 3100 True Wireless Earbuds, Sweatproof and Waterproof In Ear Workout Headphones, Grey

text_fidelity_a:
iHome iAVS16 Bedside Speaker with Alexa Built In, Bluetooth, and USB Charging, Now Supports Spotify by Voice There are both positives and negatives about this product, my perspective being that I am using it to replace an old-sko0l red LED alarm buzzer with staticy radio.

+ Looks sleeker (one would hope, as the old had a plastic wood finish), smaller footprint, and slightly raised clock makes it easier to see.

+ I love the USB port, so I can get rid of two power cords and replace it with one.

+ Shows the weather as according to Accuweather, which is at least a rough estimate of what it's like outside.

+ Better sound if you want to set it to stream music.

+ Shows the date.

+ 2 programmable buttons allow you to control "smart" devices. This could be really handy if you have a light for the room plugged into a receptacle across the room. You could also cut your overhead light cord and put in a socket for control from your bed if you're into that sort of thing. I just have a lamp beside the bed, so I really don't care, but this is something I can actually see being useful.

+ Can use it as a Bluetooth speaker. Would be better if you could integrate it with other home WiFi speakers, even though I'm more into big, hardwired speakers for serious listening from a whole-house audio system

Things that are both positive and negative, so I guess I have to call them neutral:

= microphone has a button to turn it off. A switch would be more believable, and then it wouldn't have a red light showing on the top all the time. I have no doubts the CIA can still turn it on, but I like to think the manufacturer won't listen in. I'm sure they could have put a back door in, too, but I would hope they would be sued severely if that is ever discovered. The red light is good when talking on the phone to show the phone is muted but otherwise the light shouldn't be on all the time...

= Buttons on the top are always lit up, which I consider to be a negative. Should be able to control them separately. Front display has 6 dim levels and off, and the lowest level is good for sleeping even with the thing pointed at you (at least in my opinion), but then it's really not bright enough during the day (at least if it's a bright day). I know it's petty, but I'm really not into doing anything more than I already do to get ready for bed, and that includes pressing a button 5 or 6 times to get it back to the way I wanted it. Should work on a light sensor or just be able to program it for day and evening. I mention this stuff because I'm sure it can be added via firmware (not the sensor part, obviously). Overall, not as bright as the old red LED thing, but somehow less see-able.

= You can do random light shows with the colored LEDs at the bottom. I suppose setting it to come on before your alarm is useful, but just playing with them is not.

Negatives:

- I just hate the Internet sometimes, and this reminds me why. (I'm a fairly young Systems Engineer, FYI, so it's not that I'm some geezer that can't use technology). I just hate that I need an app to control this thing. It's an alarm clock, so shouldn't I be able to do the basics without my phone? Is this just so they can get on my phone and steal my data/identity/whatever? I got news for you guys - I set this kind of crap up with a burner phone that is linked to fake Email, fake everything, location and everything else turned off. Let me at least set the bloody time without hooking up to the Internet! What happens when Comcast freezes and my WiFi temporarily doesn't have Internet connection?

To use Spotify with this (which I don't use and never will since I just have all the music I could ever want on a local server), you have to buy the Premium version. I'm sure that was absolutely necessary. Is anything not contrived multi-layered big business anymore?

Just to DL the app, Google and my burner phone both try to trick me into thinking I have to put credit card details in to get it. Sometimes I'm just ready to forego the digital age and find an old ticking clock that loses 5 minutes every day to run my life by. I am so sick and tired of adds, apps that want to control and steal your life, and companies that can't think further than next quarter...

- No battery backup. Should be built in. Even my '70s POS could be backed up via 9v battery. It saves some settings, but turns back to archaic Fahrenheit on me when power is lost...

- ...worse...when power comes back on, it screams at you. Power in my area is good, but on occasion goes out for a few seconds multiple times in a night. That may be the end of this thing (OK, I just lowered my star rating to 3, because the truth is, that probably will be the end of this thing's reign in my bedroom).

- No radio. No internal memory for music. You're at the mercy of streaming accounts and everything working properly on your network.

- Going along with the first negative point, you can't even set an alarm with this thing if you don't sign in with an Amazon account and do the Alexa thing. More ways to get grips on you. More ways to complicate a simple alarm clock.

Do I really hate simple and easy so much? I almost gave this four stars due to the fact that it looks pretty and adds some functionality, but what's wrong with a highly visible dump clock beside the bed? That's all I'm using this for, when it all comes down to it. Well, my feelings may change for the better when they inevitably fix some of the simple things on this that they can do by firmware. I will let you know if my feelings change significantly.
text_fidelity_b: iHome iAVS16 Bedside Speaker with Alexa Built In, Bluetooth, and USB Charging, Now Supports Spotify by Voice

text_fidelity_a:
RCA RCRPS06GR 6 Device Universal Remote What occurred to me after wasting half an hour with this thing is that what is needed is an iPhone app to control your television and stereo, not a single freaking light bulb and a long, long list of codes printed in mouse type.

See photo. The remote looks good, shiny Darth Vader black. There are three manuals, one of which is about an ounce and a half. One is a long list of codes and the third unfolds to about 10x17 so that between the three differently-sized printed manuals you have a lap full of clutter which is difficult to manage while you're trying to press buttons in some order.

I couldn't get it to do much of anything, and by the time I realized that half an hour had gone by and I was getting hot under the collar, I thought: FAIL. Why waste any more of my time? Ah, but by THAT time I was and am good and frustrated at this RCA product. RCA. Who knew they were still in business? Who the heck would buy an RCA product? I'm sure they made great gramophones back in the day, but Sony came by and ate their lunch and even that was forty years ago.

If you were an RCA exec, wouldn't you want to make certain that anything your company made was functional? I've got a couple college degrees. I can tie my own shoes. I can do all kinds of things, but I couldn't figure out how to program this little (EXPLETIVE DELETED) thing. Which frustrates me.

The first thing I noticed (after I cut the I-dare-you-to-open-me hard plastic packaging) was that it hurt to open the battery compartment. There's some idiotic L-shaped trigger you have to depress, meaning that you're digging it under your fingernails, which I think most people would find painful. Just a dumb design move. No other word for it. Dumb.

The remote looks good and has some interesting ribs underneath it. The buttons are not what you might expect, the volume and channel buttons are flabby feeling and weak, not definite-feeling. The center "OK" button is kind of clicky, like cellophane. There's a whole array of buttons, but it's not worth my time to try and program each one. And I grew to dislike the hard plastic feeling of the remote. There are other plastic materials that feel better to the hand. LOOK AT SONY PRODUCTS, RCA, LOOK AT SONY PRODUCTS FOR A FREE CLUE.

I'm annoyed and frustrated. This seemed like such a neat idea. But sitting on my couch juggling three differently-sized manuals AND this remote and wondering why none of these instructions were doing anything was really frustrating, just not how I want to spend my free time. I'll happily continue to exist with my TV remote, my surround-sound remote, my AppleTV remote and the AT&T cable box remote, you know? BECAUSE THEY WORK and they work without frustrating me.

Here's my idea: RCA hires an app developer and somehow figures out how to have your devices tell the app what their codes area. Something like that. Because the notion of combing through a manual full of codes in tiny type is worse than doing your income taxes.

THE WORLD HAS MOVED ON, RCA and you are apparently living in the 1970s with burgundy leisure suits and avocado-colored kitchen appliances.

STAY AWAY FROM THIS REMOTE, IT WILL ONLY FRUSTRATE YOU and dig in the skin under your nails. Ouch. Did this thing really have to be so frustrating? Do you imagine this is the kind of experience consumers are after? Not just one more freaking remote control, but one that promises convenience and delivers frustration? Not a good product. Stay away from it.
text_fidelity_b: RCA RCRPS06GR 6 Device Universal Remote

I am going to do some further testing and contact support once again about resetting this camera hopefully without having to dissemble it again but I don't see how. It has been disconnected for hours without power and will not reset that way. I also notice that the camera unit get's extremely hot for some reason. This will defiantly shorten it's life span. More to come on this product but for now I do not recommend buying this unless you are familiar with IP camera installation, network configuration, and have some electrical experience as far as handling circuit boards. HP 20-inch LED (1600 X 900) LED Backlit Monitor with VGA & DVI-D Port (W2082a, Black) - L8K84AA#ABA This is a decent PC monitor that doesn’t excel in any area but, at the same time, doesn’t fall flat either (except for sound quality). It’s a good choice if you’re looking for an inexpensive, wide-screen monitor that comes in at under $100.

The build quality is what you’d expect at this price point: pretty basic and simple. The casing is all plastic, and rather cheap feeling plastic at that. It comes with a very basic stand that allows a limited amount of tilt adjustment, but no swivel or monitor rotation. There are no mounting holes on the back to facilitate a wall or stand mount. There are also no convenience features, such as a USB hub. It also lacks an HDMI port.

On the plus side, the power cord just plugs into the monitor without the need for a transformer or wall wart. The overall monitor profile is pretty slim, and it is very lightweight.

Setup is very simple. No tools are needed to attach the stand (just push and it clicks into place). It comes with a VGA cable, a 3.5mm audio cable and a power cable. Although it includes a DVI port, it does not come with the cable to use that. It also does not come with a user guide (other than a one-page quick setup sheet) or a driver disk. Both are available as downloads from the HP site. However, neither are really needed.

I hooked it up to my laptop via VGA to use as a secondary monitor. It auto installed under Win 7, so it should be able to do the same for 8 and 10. The recommended resolution is 1600x900 at 60Htz.

Right out of the box the settings were eye-searing bright, as is typical with manufacturer defaults since they want their monitors to stand out when on display in a store. Changing the settings is pretty easy – the menu button brings up the full list of options; you select the one you want; then adjust with the +/- keys. You can experiment at will since there’s also a choice to return to factory defaults should you get lost in the weeds with changes. The adjustment menu is pretty extensive for a monitor at this price point. You can adjust the usual brightness and contrast, and also color temp, image control, and even turn off the blue LED power indicator (yes!). Unfortunately, the control button labels are impossible to read (black on black) but there’s only a few buttons, so it's not tough to figure out.

The image quality is decent once it’s been properly adjusted. It won’t wow you, but it provides good performance on both images and text. I was happier with the text performance than I was with video (it has pretty limited black levels) but, for an everyday, inexpensive monitor, it’s more than acceptable.

The speakers are very, very basic. Tinny to the point of being useless. I’ve gotten better sound out of a $5 set of basic computer speakers.

I’m giving this 4 stars since, even at this price point, HP could have done a better job with the overall look/feel of the monitor, have included some additional convenience features such as a swivel, USB hub, and/or an HDMI port. Features that could have been dropped are the internal speakers, which are useless for anything other than to hear system beeps. Still, even as-is, it’s worth considering if you’re looking for a no-frills, no-fuss, inexpensive monitor.
text_fidelity_b: HP 20-inch LED (1600 X 900) LED Backlit Monitor with VGA & DVI-D Port (W2082a, Black) - L8K84AA#ABA
